# Results — Study 386 (NFCI-Conditions)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The Chicago Fed's **National
Financial Conditions Index (NFCI)** — a weekly z-score where **positive = tighter-than-average
financial conditions** — is folklore-famous as a regime switch for equities: *"when conditions
turn tight, step out of stocks."* The true NFCI lives only on FRED (`NFCI`), which is **not
reachable from this environment**, so we build a **transparent financial-conditions proxy** from
yfinance instruments and test the claim on it. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance weekly closes — `^GSPC`, `^VIX`, `^MOVE`, `LQD`, `IEF`, `UUP` (public, no key) |
| As-of | **2026-06-22** (last completed week ending **2026-06-19**; partial week dropped) |
| Window | 2002-01-04 → 2026-06-19 (**1,277** weeks; **24.5** years) |
| Conditions proxy | z-score of {equity vol, rates vol, IG-vs-Treasury credit spread, broad-dollar momentum}; **high = tight** (NFCI's sign); **PROXY** for the Chicago Fed NFCI |
| Tightness cut | `fci >= +0.5 z` (top ~tercile) → "tight"; **271** tight weeks (21%) |
| Entry / costs | 1-week execution lag; one-way 5 bps charged per switch in the timing rule |

> **Proxy caveat (named on the Signal axis).** The true NFCI bundles ~100 series (money,
> debt and equity markets); our four-leg yfinance proxy is **narrower and noisier**, starts in
> 2002 (`LQD`/`IEF`/`^MOVE`), and is built partly from equity volatility — so it is
> *mechanically* glued to stocks. We never call it the NFCI; the verdict rests on the
> **forward** (predictive) link, which the proxy estimates honestly with a 1-week lag, not on
> the contemporaneous link, which is near-tautological for *any* vol-laden conditions index
> (the genuine NFCI included).

## The mechanical trap — tight weeks *are* down weeks (and that's not a signal)

The week-over-week change in the conditions proxy correlates **−0.73** with the same week's
S&P return. That looks like a killer timing signal until you notice it is *contemporaneous*:
the index embeds equity volatility, so "conditions tightened this week" and "stocks fell this
week" are two names for one event. You cannot trade a coincidence. The only tradable question
is the **forward** one — does tightness *today* beat the base rate for *next* week/month?

## The signal — forward S&P returns after a tight week vs the base rate

1-week entry lag; the unconditional column is *all* overlapping forward windows over the same
tape (the honest base rate). Welch *t* compares the tight-week conditional mean to the
unconditional mean; the placebo *p* is the share of 20,000 random same-size week draws whose
mean forward return is **at or below** the tight set (i.e. how often chance looks as bearish).

| horizon | n tight | cond. mean | cond. win-rate | base mean | base win-rate | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-week  | 271 | **+0.08%** | 53% | +0.18% | 57% | **−0.38** | 0.264 |
| 4-week  | 271 | **+0.66%** | 58% | +0.70% | 64% | **−0.09** | 0.443 |
| 13-week | 269 | **+1.72%** | 62% | +2.22% | 70% | **−0.70** | 0.134 |

Read it carefully. After a tight week the market's forward return is **slightly below** the
base rate at every horizon — the *direction* the folklore predicts (tight ⇒ weaker forward
returns) — but the gap is tiny and **none of it clears the desk's t ≥ 2 bar**: the most
negative is 13-week at **t = −0.70 / placebo p = 0.13**. Tightness shaves a little off forward
returns; it does not call a top. The lore's "step out of stocks" punch is essentially the
contemporaneous −0.73 worn as if it were foresight.

## The timing rule — a real Sharpe bump, but it's volatility, not alpha

Step out of stocks (hold cash) the week after the proxy is tight, otherwise hold the S&P;
1-week lag, one-way costs on each switch, raced excess-of-cash vs buy-and-hold.

| cost | switches | % in cash | strat Sharpe (vol) | B&H Sharpe (vol) | Sharpe gap | strat CAGR | B&H CAGR |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps  | 90 | 21% | **0.71** (11.7%) | 0.53 (17.2%) | **+0.18** | 7.8% | 7.8% |
| 5 bps  | 90 | 21% | **0.69** (11.7%) | 0.53 (17.2%) | **+0.16** | 7.6% | 7.8% |
| 10 bps | 90 | 21% | **0.67** (11.7%) | 0.53 (17.2%) | **+0.15** | 7.4% | 7.8% |

The rule *does* lift Sharpe (0.69 vs 0.53 net of 5 bps). But look at the engine: **the CAGR is
the same (~7.7%)** — the rule earns no extra return; it just **cuts volatility from 17.2% to
11.7%** by sitting out the highest-vol weeks. That is the *contemporaneous* −0.73 leaking
forward through the one-week persistence of volatility (high-vol weeks cluster), not a forecast
of direction. It is a **risk-reduction overlay**, not an edge — and a leveraged buy-and-hold at
matched vol would erase the Sharpe gap.

## Robustness — the gap is regime-concentrated and statistically fragile

| check | result |
|---|---|
| Drop the 2008-09 crisis | Sharpe gap **+0.164 → +0.091** (roughly halves) |
| Block-bootstrap 90% CI on the Sharpe gap | **−0.09 to +0.43** (straddles zero; ~15% of resamples ≤ 0) |
| Threshold 0.0 / 0.5 / 1.0 z (13-wk *t*) | −1.17 / −0.70 / +0.08 — **never reaches −2**, and the sign of the point estimate **flips** at the tightest cut |

The timing bump is mostly one crisis (2008), its bootstrap interval includes zero, and the
forward *t* never clears the bar at any threshold. There is no cut at which "step out when
tight" becomes a robust, deployable edge.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, and contemporaneous ≠ predictive

On a deterministic conditions index whose price has a **strong contemporaneous** coupling
(transient tightness shocks hit the *same* week's return, like the real index) and a
**separately planted forward edge** on the persistent regime:

| planted forward edge | contemp corr | cond 13w mean | base 13w mean | Welch *t* | placebo *p* | timing Sharpe gap |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.000** (none) | −0.27 | +2.15% | +2.06% | **+0.19** | 0.592 | **−0.24** |
| **0.006** (moderate) | −0.23 | −0.47% | +1.67% | **−3.94** | 0.000 | +0.46 |
| **0.012** (large) | −0.17 | −2.78% | +1.62% | **−5.89** | 0.000 | +1.06 |

With **no** planted forward edge the forward test sits at **t = +0.19** (no false positive) and
the timing rule has a *negative* Sharpe gap — even though the **contemporaneous correlation is a
healthy −0.27**, exactly the real-tape pattern. Only when a genuine forward edge is planted does
the forward *t* light up. The control proves two things at once: the engine is unbiased, **and**
a strong contemporaneous link manufactures **no** forward signal — which is precisely why the
real tape's −0.73 coincidence and its near-zero forward *t* are not a contradiction.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** Tightness is correctly *signed* against forward returns (the lore's
  direction), but the forward effect is tiny and **fails t ≥ 2** at every horizon (13-week
  t = −0.70, placebo p = 0.13) and **flips sign** at the tightest threshold. The eye-catching
  −0.73 is **contemporaneous** (the index embeds equity vol) and carries no foresight.
  Direction-right, significance-absent ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL. (Proxy + survivorship-light named
  on this axis.)
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** "Step out when tight" *does* raise Sharpe (0.69 vs 0.53) — but
  purely by **cutting vol** (17.2% → 11.7%) at the **same CAGR**, the bump **halves** ex-2008,
  and its bootstrap CI straddles zero. A vol-reduction overlay a leverage-matched benchmark
  would neutralise is **not** a NAV-scale edge.
- **"Step out of stocks?" — MISATTRIBUTED.** The signal's apparent power is the index *being
  built from* the thing it claims to predict — a contemporaneous coincidence dressed as a
  forecast. A conditions index tells you it is *raining now*, not that it will rain next week.
